title: Spinal Opioids in Anesthetic Practice -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Regional anesthesia has evolved into a safe and effective technique, with spinal opioids playing a central role in postoperative and chronic pain management. Once considered high-risk, advances in sterile technique, drug formulation, and evidence from large-scale studies have established spinal anesthesia as a reliable option for surgical and analgesic purposes. This course reviews intrathecal opioids, eg, morphine, fentanyl, and sufentanil, which provide superior pain control by enhancing sensory block quality and reducing systemic opioid requirements. Participants will also gain an understanding of their pharmacologic differences—particularly between hydrophilic and lipophilic agents—to inform clinical decision-making, balancing onset, duration, and adverse effect profiles. Despite the potential for complications such as pruritus, postdural puncture headache, and dose-dependent respiratory depression, spinal opioids remain a valuable tool when appropriately selected and monitored.

title: Spinal Opioids in Anesthetic Practice -- Introduction
content: Regional anesthesia, consisting of spinal, caudal, and epidural blocks, was first utilized for surgical procedures at the turn of the twentieth century. Initially deemed unsafe due to reports of permanent neurologic injury, a large-scale study in the 1950s proved complications were rare when blocks were performed skillfully and with attention to sterile technique, combined with the improved safety profile of injected medications. Initial work showing improved pain management in cancer patients has expanded spinal opioids for postoperative pain management. [1]

title: Spinal Opioids in Anesthetic Practice -- Introduction
content: Spinal anesthesia has developed a well-established record of safety over decades of clinical use. In certain situations, clinicians regard it as the anesthetic of choice and, in select cases, the safest available option. Local anesthetics provide the foundation for surgical anesthesia, yet they are frequently paired with intrathecal opioids to enhance intraoperative analgesia and extend pain relief into the postoperative period once the local anesthetic effect diminishes.

title: Spinal Opioids in Anesthetic Practice -- Introduction
content: Intrathecal opioids deliver effective analgesia while avoiding sympathetic and motor blockade, offering targeted pain control with fewer physiologic disruptions. Their utility extends beyond perioperative care into the management of chronic pain. Clinicians may administer them as single injections for select patients, but more commonly employ implantable infusion pumps to deliver sustained, long-term relief in individuals with complex pain syndromes.

title: Spinal Opioids in Anesthetic Practice -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Vertebral Anatomy
content: The spine consists of vertebral bones separated by intervertebral discs, providing both structure and flexibility,  comprising 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, and 5 lumbar vertebrae, followed by the sacrum. Posterior vertebral elements consist of the vertebral arch, spinous process, pedicles, and laminae, while the vertebral body forms the anterior portion. Thoracic spinous processes angle steeply and project inferiorly, whereas lumbar spinous processes extend in a nearly horizontal orientation. At each vertebral level, paired spinal nerves exit the central nervous system (CNS), contributing to peripheral innervation.

title: Spinal Opioids in Anesthetic Practice -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Vertebral Anatomy
content: The spinal cord occupies the vertebral column and is enclosed by the pia mater, arachnoid mater, and dura mater. Teaching emphasizes that the spinal cord extends from the foramen magnum to L1 in adults and to L3 in children, migrating cephalad with age. A lumbar puncture performed below L1 in adults or below L3 in children minimizes the risk of needle trauma. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) fills the subarachnoid or intrathecal space, accessed through successive layers: skin, subcutaneous fat, supraspinous ligament, interspinous ligament, ligamentum flavum, dura mater, subdural space, arachnoid mater, and finally the subarachnoid space.

title: Spinal Opioids in Anesthetic Practice -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Vertebral Anatomy
content: CSF circulates within the cerebral ventricles, cisterns, and subarachnoid space, cushioning the CNS and clearing metabolic waste. The choroid plexuses of the lateral ventricles produce most CSF, with smaller contributions from ventricular ependymal linings and perivascular fluid exchange. In adults, CSF production averages 21 mL/h, maintaining a total volume of approximately 150 mL. Flow proceeds from the lateral ventricles through the intraventricular foramina into the third ventricle, then via the cerebral aqueduct into the fourth ventricle, and exits through the foramen of Magendie and foramina of Luschka into the cerebellomedullary cistern. From this point, CSF enters the subarachnoid space, circulating around the brain and spinal cord before absorption through arachnoid granulations. CSF remains isotonic with plasma but contains lower concentrations of potassium, bicarbonate, and glucose, as well as limited protein. Absorption serves as the principal mechanism for returning perivascular and interstitial protein to the blood, compensating for the absence of lymphatics in the CNS.

title: Spinal Opioids in Anesthetic Practice -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Pharmacology
content: Opioids used in spinal anesthesia can be broadly categorized as hydrophilic or lipophilic. Lipophilic opioids demonstrate a rapid onset of action, diffuse quickly into surrounding tissues, and produce a shorter duration of effect with minimal rostral spread. Their primary role involves prolonging the sensory block of intrathecal local anesthetics. Hydrophilic opioids, in contrast, act more slowly but exhibit prolonged rostral spread above the injection site and slower plasma reuptake, resulting in broader distribution and extended analgesia.

title: Spinal Opioids in Anesthetic Practice -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Pharmacology
content: Five opioid receptor types have been characterized: mu (MOR), kappa (KOR), delta (DOR), nociception (NOR), and zeta (ZOR). ZOR regulates tissue growth events, while the other four contribute to analgesia. Both endogenous and exogenous opioids bind to these G-protein-coupled receptors, leading to the inhibition of voltage-gated calcium channels and the suppression of excitatory neurotransmitters, eg, substance P and glutamate. [2]

title: Spinal Opioids in Anesthetic Practice -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Pharmacology
content: Morphine remains the most frequently used neuraxial opioid because of its long duration compared with fentanyl and sufentanil. Diamorphine, used almost exclusively in the UK, is 280 times more lipid soluble than morphine, which accounts for its shorter onset. Morphine binds primarily to mu-opioid receptor subtypes mu1 and mu2, inhibiting adenylate cyclase through G-protein signaling. [3] This action increases potassium channel activity while suppressing voltage-dependent calcium channels, raising the threshold for neuronal pain transmission. [4] Morphine stimulates opioid receptors in the substantia gelatinosa of the posterior spinal cord, and its hydrophilic nature enables slow rostral spread with prolonged analgesia, even when delivered at the lumbar level. [5] [6] [5] Intrathecal morphine provides approximately 18 to 24 hours of postoperative pain relief, with an onset of 45 to 75 minutes due to limited penetration across the blood-brain barrier. Adult dosing typically ranges from 0.15 to 0.3 mg.

[7] Their lipophilic properties account for a rapid onset, typically 5 to 20 minutes, with durations of 1 to 4 hours for fentanyl and 2 to 6 hours for sufentanil. Morphine, by contrast, remains concentrated at the dorsal horn of the spinal cord due to slower uptake, providing more sustained spinal-level analgesia.

title: Spinal Opioids in Anesthetic Practice -- Indications -- Perioperative Indications for Spinal Opioids
content: When combined with a local anesthetic, spinal opioids improve the block's quality and reduce the need for systemic opioids postoperatively. For procedures that begin rapidly after a spinal injection, eg, cesarean section, fentanyl (10 to 20 µg) is often added due to its rapid onset to improve analgesia during surgery, while intrathecal morphine is added to provide postoperative analgesia. During the cesarean section, the addition of spinal opioids to the local anesthetic helps block discomfort due to the manipulation of the uterus. For surgeries that require large incisions or median sternotomy, fentanyl may or may not be added, and intrathecal morphine is added to provide postoperative analgesia.

title: Spinal Opioids in Anesthetic Practice -- Indications -- Chronic Pain Management With Spinal Opioids
content: Intrathecal opioids have a place in treating cancer pain refractory to systemic opioids, nonopioid analgesics, and other nonpharmacologic pain treatments. Intrathecal administration is preferred over the epidural route as drug doses required via epidural are approximately 10 times higher and increase systemic adverse effects. [8] Implantable intrathecal infusion systems are available that deliver drugs to the CNS. The intrathecal catheter is typically placed below L1 under fluoroscopy. The decision to implant a pump is made based on priorities of patient care and life expectancy. In patients with severe chronic pain, comfort should be the priority. If life expectancy is weeks to months, a catheter may be tunneled under the skin and connected to a subcutaneous port. If life expectancy is longer, fully implanted catheters and infusion pumps are selected. Both fixed-rate and programmable pumps that provide as-needed bolus doses are available. If an intrathecal infusion pump is considered, a trial is often performed first with a single-shot technique. [9]

content: The decision to administer spinal opioids for chronic pain management should be made after confirmation that more conventional treatments are ineffective. [10] Furthermore, as with all chronic pain management, the clinician must perform a thorough assessment of the source of pain and its impact on daily living activities. Imaging studies may aid the decision regarding the pain management technique to be selected and are vital to rule out sources of pain that should be treated surgically, eg, a tumor compressing a nerve.

title: Spinal Opioids in Anesthetic Practice -- Indications -- Spinal Opioid Benefits
content: Neuraxial blockade applied for surgery has been shown to reduce postoperative mortality and additional serious complications after surgery. These include deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, and respiratory depression, as well as transfusion requirements. [11] Inadequate analgesia during the postoperative period can also lead to numerous adverse consequences, including hemodynamic instability (tachycardia, hypertension, vasoconstriction), increased catabolism, impaired immune response, and altered platelet activation. [12] [13] These are particularly undesirable in patients with numerous preexisting comorbidities or following cardiac surgery.

title: Spinal Opioids in Anesthetic Practice -- Indications -- Spinal Opioid Benefits
content: The addition of opioids to local anesthetics intensifies the quality of the sensory block produced by local anesthetics alone. When appropriately used, intrathecal opioids provide analgesia that is often superior to that achieved via the epidural and intravenous (IV) routes. Furthermore, when used in appropriate (low) doses, intrathecal opioids result in an adverse effect profile similar to that of systemic opioids, with an exception: pruritus tends to occur more commonly with intrathecal opioids. Finally, a spinal is easier to perform than an epidural.

title: Spinal Opioids in Anesthetic Practice -- Contraindications -- Absolute Contraindications
content: Before performing spinal anesthesia, clinicians should obtain a thorough history to screen for the presence of contraindications, including questions about mucosal bleeding, unusual bleeding after trauma, dental procedures, or surgery, as well as significant nosebleeds or heavy menstrual bleeding. The presence of petechiae, ecchymoses, or a history of abnormal bleeding warrants hematology consultation before proceeding. In the absence of such a history, spinal anesthesia can generally be performed if prothrombin time (PT), activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), and platelet count are normal, as these tests exclude most clinically relevant bleeding disorders. Nonetheless, mild forms of von Willebrand disease may remain undetected.

title: Spinal Opioids in Anesthetic Practice -- Contraindications -- Absolute Contraindications
content: However, no universally accepted platelet threshold exists below which spinal anesthesia should never be performed, and practice varies among clinicians, institutions, and patient populations. Older literature recommended a platelet count of at least 100×10 9 /L, but many practitioners now consider lower counts acceptable depending on the indication and overall clinical context. For instance, in patients with cancer experiencing severe pain or in obstetric patients where general anesthesia poses high risks due to morbid obesity or abnormal airway anatomy, the benefits of spinal anesthesia may outweigh the risks. In parturients without preeclampsia, some propose a safe threshold of 75×10 9 /L, while reports from Douglas et al (2001) and Tanaka et al describe successful spinal procedures with platelet counts below 75×10 9 /L in patients with idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) or gestational thrombocytopenia. These studies suggest that in nonpreeclamptic parturients without a history or signs of bleeding, counts as low as 50×10 9 /L may be acceptable. [15]

title: Spinal Opioids in Anesthetic Practice -- Contraindications -- Relative Contraindications
content: Relative contraindications to spinal anesthesia should be evaluated on an individual basis, with risks weighed against potential benefits. Conditions such as spinal stenosis, prior spinal surgery, and spina bifida present challenges because altered anatomy can complicate needle placement and produce unpredictable spread of local anesthetic. [20] Reports have described an association between neuraxial techniques and nerve injury in patients with spinal stenosis, lumbar disk disease, or a history of spine surgery. [20] However, this link cannot be considered causal, since the data come from a retrospective study without a control group of surgical patients who did not undergo neuraxial techniques, and confounding factors such as disease progression were not accounted for. Patients with multiple sclerosis may demonstrate variable responses to spinal anesthesia, sometimes experiencing prolonged motor or sensory blockade, yet evidence does not suggest that spinal anesthesia worsens disease symptoms. [21]

title: Spinal Opioids in Anesthetic Practice -- Contraindications -- Relative Contraindications
content: Bacteremia is also considered by some to represent a relative contraindication, primarily due to concerns that a needle traversing a blood vessel might introduce bacteria into the epidural or subarachnoid space. Nonetheless, clinicians frequently perform diagnostic lumbar punctures in patients with a fever of unknown origin. Available evidence indicates that lumbar puncture does not increase the risk of meningitis compared with the incidence of spontaneous meningitis. Cases labeled as lumbar puncture–induced meningitis may actually represent meningitis from subsequent hematogenous seeding in patients with significant bacteremia. [22] These findings support the view that spinal anesthesia can be performed when judged safer than general anesthesia, particularly if the patient has already demonstrated a clinical response to antibiotic therapy initiated before spinal puncture. [23] In children younger than 1 year, however, studies have reported a higher incidence of meningitis following lumbar puncture during bacteremia, underscoring the need for heightened caution in this population. [24]

title: Spinal Opioids in Anesthetic Practice -- Contraindications -- Hemodynamic Considerations
content: Hypovolemia, hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, and mitral stenosis represent relative contraindications to spinal anesthesia with local anesthetics. In these conditions, spinal-induced reductions in systemic vascular resistance can precipitate profound hypotension in patients who depend heavily on preload. Severe aortic stenosis requires even greater caution, as spinal injection of local anesthetic should be regarded as contraindicated. Patients with severe aortic stenosis have hypertrophied left ventricles with elevated oxygen demands, and reductions in diastolic blood pressure and coronary perfusion pressure may trigger myocardial ischemia. In select cases of mild or moderate valvular heart disease, low-dose intrathecal opioid administration without local anesthetic may be tolerated, as this produces smaller reductions in blood pressure. However, spinal techniques should be avoided in severe aortic stenosis, because once ventricular fibrillation occurs in this population, resuscitation is extremely difficult or impossible.

title: Spinal Opioids in Anesthetic Practice -- Preparation
content: History and coagulation tests should be used to exclude the possibility of a bleeding disorder. Questions related to drug ingestion should be asked as well, as medications may increase bleeding risk. The clinician should inquire about large-volume alcohol ingestion, as alcohol potentiates aspirin-induced and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug-induced prolonged bleeding time for up to 2 days. [26] Spinal can usually be performed safely if patients take 325 mg of aspirin daily or a low dose of a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug. Notably, the number of days that drugs should be discontinued before regional anesthesia varies for different anticoagulants, antiplatelet agents, and herbal agents, based on their pharmacology. Therefore, the practitioner should refer to the 2018 guidelines of the American Society of Regional Anesthesia and Pain Medicine to ensure a safe amount of time has passed. [27]

title: Spinal Opioids in Anesthetic Practice -- Preparation -- Day of Procedure
content: Preparatory steps for spinal anesthesia remain consistent whether opioids are added to local anesthetic for surgery or administered alone in the pain management setting for chronic pain. Informed consent must always be obtained and should include a clear explanation of the risks and benefits of the spinal procedure. Patients should be advised about both mild adverse effects, such as nausea and pruritus, and more serious complications, including headache and neurologic injury. Postdural puncture headache (PDPH) occurs in approximately 1.5% to 2% of young, pregnant women, though newer studies report incidences as high as 4%. Persistent PDPH has led to medicolegal claims, making it important to explain the risk thoroughly to parturients. Patients should also be informed that spinal anesthesia for cesarean section is safer than general anesthesia, and that effective treatments, including epidural blood patch, are available if PDPH develops.

title: Spinal Opioids in Anesthetic Practice -- Technique or Treatment
content: When spinal anesthesia is used to supplement general anesthesia for major surgery, the placement usually occurs while the patient remains awake. This allows the patient to report pain or paresthesia, which may alert the anesthesiologist that the needle has contacted a nerve root. A slight withdrawal of the needle may then prevent intraneural injection, a factor some believe reduces the likelihood of postoperative neurologic complications, although the evidence remains inconclusive. In children, spinal anesthesia is frequently performed under general anesthesia, and no convincing evidence suggests this practice increases neurologic risk.

title: Spinal Opioids in Anesthetic Practice -- Technique or Treatment
content: The choice between sitting and lateral decubitus positioning lacks clear superiority, though the midline landmark is typically easier to identify in the sitting posture. In this position, patients sit with their back perpendicular to the table, resting their elbows on a support or hugging a pillow, while flexing their spine to open the interspaces. An assistant often helps maintain the posture and encourages maximal lumbar flexion. In the lateral decubitus position, patients adopt a fetal posture with knees drawn toward the chest and neck flexed, which also enhances interspace exposure. Anatomical landmarks guide introducer placement, with an imaginary line drawn across the iliac crests most often aligning with the L4 spinous process or the L4-L5 interspace. However, a puncture may occasionally occur at adjacent levels. Spinous processes generally mark the midline, while the intergluteal cleft may assist in obese patients where palpation proves difficult.

title: Spinal Opioids in Anesthetic Practice -- Technique or Treatment
content: Whether a single-shot spinal or continuous catheter is chosen, two primary insertion techniques—midline and paramedian—are available. After skin preparation with an antiseptic solution and application of a sterile fenestrated drape, local infiltration, usually with lidocaine 1% to 2%, anesthetizes the insertion site. The introducer is advanced at a 10 to 15 degrees cephalad angle, followed by passage of the spinal needle (commonly 24–27 gauge) with its bevel parallel to the midline. Distinct tactile feedback occurs as the needle traverses the ligaments, with a characteristic “pop” felt on dural penetration. The average insertion depth in adults is about 5 cm. [31]

content: If the midline approach fails due to arthritis, kyphoscoliosis, previous surgery, or calcified ligaments, a paramedian technique may be used. Here, the needle enters 1 cm caudal and 1 cm lateral to the tip of the L4 spinous process, angled 10 to 15 degrees cephalad and medially, thereby bypassing the supraspinous and interspinous ligaments. After dural puncture, clear CSF confirms correct placement before medication injection. Occasionally, blood-stained CSF appears initially but clears with continued flow, and injection may proceed in such cases. [32]

Effective pharmacologic treatments include IV meperidine, tramadol, and clonidine.

title: Spinal Opioids in Anesthetic Practice -- Complications -- Adverse Effects
content: Adverse effects of spinal opioids, including nausea, vomiting, urinary retention, pruritus, and respiratory depression, mirror those seen with intravenous administration, though pruritus is often more pronounced with intrathecal delivery. Historical reports of severe respiratory depression and arrest involved excessive intrathecal opioid doses. Most adverse effects are dose-dependent; intrathecal morphine doses above 0.5 mg carry a higher risk. [35] Pruritus is particularly pronounced with sufentanil compared with fentanyl, contributing to fentanyl’s more frequent use. [36] Small doses of naloxone, 40 to 80 µg, effectively reduce pruritus without reversing analgesia, and ondansetron also diminishes severity. [37] Neuraxial opioids may induce urinary retention via spinal and pontine micturition centers. [38]

content: Respiratory depression presents a serious concern due to its potentially life-threatening yet often insidious nature. No universal definition exists; however, clinical surrogates include decreased respiratory rate, oxygen saturation below 92%, the need for supplemental oxygen or airway intervention, and sedation requiring more than verbal stimulation. Patients may appear comfortable while hypercarbia contributes to subtle hypoventilation. Respiratory depression from intrathecal morphine typically occurs 6 to 18 hours after injection, though earlier onset can occur with concomitant IV narcotics. Low intraoperative and postoperative intravenous opioid dosing is advised when intrathecal morphine is administered. Evidence supports effective analgesia with intrathecal morphine doses as low as 0.15 to 0.3 mg for pelvic or abdominal surgery and 0.3 mg for median sternotomy. Postoperative patient-controlled analgesia with low-dose IV fentanyl or morphine optimizes pain control while minimizing risk. For same-day surgical procedures, intrathecal fentanyl should be limited to 5 to 10 µg. Continuous monitoring of patients receiving intrathecal morphine remains essential to detect and manage potential respiratory depression.

Causes of block failure include needle movement during injection, incomplete entry of the needle into the subarachnoid space, or inadvertent injection into a nerve root. If a spinal with local anesthetic fails, proceeding with general anesthesia is advisable. Attempting a second dose may result in a high spinal, which carries risks of severe hypotension, bradycardia, respiratory arrest, and cardiac arrest.

title: Spinal Opioids in Anesthetic Practice -- Clinical Significance
content: Intrathecal opioids, whether combined with local anesthetics for surgical anesthesia or administered alone, blunt the intraoperative stress response, reduce the requirement for anesthetic agents, and enhance postoperative analgesia. Low-dose fentanyl, 10 to 20 µg, is commonly added to local anesthetics for short or minimally invasive procedures, whereas intrathecal morphine is typically used for surgeries involving larger incisions. Administration of intrathecal opioids is straightforward, requiring no specialized equipment or advanced technical skills. title: Spinal Opioids in Anesthetic Practice -- Clinical Significance -- Cesarean Section
content: Neuraxial anaesthesia is the preferred technique for caesarean deliveries in the United States and Canada, used for more than 95% of these procedures. [46] A combination of local anaesthetic (most often bupivacaine) and opioid (fentanyl and morphine) is frequently used. Other opioids, eg, diamorphine, mepredine, sufentanyl, have been described for intrathecal use during caesarean section. A meta-analysis of patients undergoing spinal anaesthesia for cesarean section found the need for intraoperative analgesic supplementation decreased from 24% to 4% when opioids were added to the local anaesthetic injection. [7] The preference for spinal (or epidural) anaesthesia over general anaesthesia is that regional techniques preclude the need to manage the airway, which is more challenging in the pregnant population. Furthermore, maternal blood loss is decreased with spinal compared to general anesthesia, primarily due to lower blood pressure. [47] Spinal anaesthesia also allows the mother to be awake, have a partner present, and permits rapid bonding with the baby. Fentanyl 10 to 15 µg is often administered to supplement intraoperative analgesia provided by the local anaesthetic, while it is added to 0.100 to 0.150 mg intrathecal morphine to provide postoperative analgesia.

title: Spinal Opioids in Anesthetic Practice -- Clinical Significance -- Cardiac Procedures
content: Multiple groups have reported the use of intrathecal morphine in patients undergoing cardiac surgery. title: Spinal Opioids in Anesthetic Practice -- Clinical Significance -- Video-Assisted Thoracoscopic Surgery
content: Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery represents a minimally invasive approach to thoracic procedures, offering advantages such as fewer pulmonary complications and faster recovery. Thoracic epidurals and fascial plane blocks are commonly used for analgesia, though both techniques present technical challenges. In contrast, single-shot intrathecal morphine provides a simpler and highly effective method of pain control in these patients. [56]

title: Spinal Opioids in Anesthetic Practice -- Clinical Significance -- Monitoring After Administration of Spinal Opioids
content: Patients who receive intrathecal morphine require close monitoring of respiratory rate and level of alertness. Standard practice involves hourly assessments for the first 12 hours, followed by evaluations every 2 hours from hours 12 to 24. Patients with comorbidities such as hypertension, cardiac or neurologic disease, body mass index of 40 or greater, use of sedatives, exposure to general anesthesia, or IV magnesium should undergo hourly monitoring for 24 hours. High-risk patients may benefit from the addition of capnometry or pulse oximetry, though clinicians must recognize that desaturation often develops late in patients receiving supplemental oxygen. Slowing respiratory rate and increasing sedation frequently signal respiratory depression earlier. A respiratory rate of 10 breaths per minute warrants immediate bedside evaluation, and order sets should mandate clinician notification at or below this threshold. Obese patients, particularly those with obstructive sleep apnea or concomitant sedative use, face a higher risk of respiratory depression and should be monitored for extended periods. [60]

title: Spinal Opioids in Anesthetic Practice -- Clinical Significance -- Monitoring After Administration of Spinal Opioids
content: For obstetric patients, the American Society of Obstetric Anesthesia and Perinatology published less restrictive guidelines in 2019 to avoid unnecessary withholding of intrathecal morphine in settings where monitoring may not be available. These guidelines apply primarily to cesarean patients, who are typically young, healthy, and receive a single intrathecal morphine dose without additional sedation. No extra monitoring is recommended when the dose is less than 50 µg. For doses between 50 µg and 150 µg, respiratory rate and sedation should be checked every 2 hours for 12 hours. For doses above 150 µg, the standard monitoring outlined above applies.

title: Spinal Opioids in Anesthetic Practice -- Clinical Significance -- Clinical Pearls
content: Traditional teaching places the termination of the adult spinal cord at L1, yet ultrasound imaging has demonstrated the conus medullaris extending below L1 in some individuals. Furthermore, palpation of the iliac crest, often assumed to represent the L4-L5 interspace, may occasionally correspond to a more cephalad level, potentially explaining episodes of paresthesia during spinal anesthesia. Symptoms, eg, nausea, dizziness, or a sensation of feeling strange shortly after spinal anesthesia, often reflect hypotension not yet measured by the monitor. Administering a small dose of phenylephrine or ephedrine—selected based on heart rate—while the blood pressure cuff cycles can correct hypotension if present and poses little risk if not.

title: Spinal Opioids in Anesthetic Practice -- Clinical Significance -- Clinical Pearls
content: During the postoperative night, reliance on pulse oximetry alone may provide false reassurance, as patients on supplemental oxygen can maintain saturations despite a dangerously slow respiratory rate. Orders should mandate clinician notification if the respiratory rate falls below 10 breaths/min. Naloxone should be administered at 40 µg IV for a respiratory rate of 8 breaths/min, with an additional 80 µg IV if the rate does not increase to at least 10 breaths/min within 2 minutes. Patients with decreased arousal should undergo arterial blood gas testing; if carbon dioxide pressure is elevated, low-dose naloxone infusion or ventilatory support (eg, BiPAP or controlled ventilation) may be necessary.

title: Spinal Opioids in Anesthetic Practice -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Spinal anesthesia, often combined with intrathecal opioids, provides effective surgical anesthesia and prolonged postoperative pain relief with a long-established record of safety. By supplementing local anesthetics, spinal opioids enhance analgesia without producing sympathetic or motor blockade, making them valuable in both perioperative and chronic pain management. Their use requires careful consideration of pharmacologic properties, patient factors, and potential adverse effects to ensure safe and effective outcomes.

title: Spinal Opioids in Anesthetic Practice -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Optimal patient-centered care relies on coordinated skills and responsibilities across the interprofessional team. Physicians and advanced practitioners must assess indications, contraindications, and dosing strategies, while nurses provide vigilant monitoring for complications such as respiratory depression or pruritus. Pharmacists contribute expertise in drug selection, interactions, and patient education. General practitioners support continuity of care, especially in the management of chronic pain, while other allied health professionals reinforce patient engagement and promote functional recovery. Effective communication and shared decision-making among team members ensure safe analgesic delivery, reduce risks, and enhance outcomes. This collaborative strategy strengthens patient safety, optimizes postoperative recovery, and supports long-term pain control.
